questions.title: Defining 'repeat purchase rate'
questions.prompt: The head of an online pet-supplies shop asks for a 'repeat purchase rate' on the weekly dashboard. Define it precisely, and explain the choices you made.
hints: Repeat within what time window, measured from when?
Which customers belong in the denominator?
What about returns, cancelled orders, subscriptions and gift purchases?
followups: The rate jumped after a subscription launch. Is that real repeat behaviour?
How would you show it weekly when the window is 60 days?
What would make this metric misleading?
criteria: States the question the metric answers.
Defines numerator, denominator, window and cohort precisely.
Handles edge cases (cancellations, returns, subscriptions, duplicate accounts).
Chooses a reporting approach for a lagging window (cohorts).
Names how the metric could mislead.
outline: Question: do new customers come back to buy again?
Cohort: customers whose first completed order was in week W.
Numerator: of those, customers with a second completed, non-refunded order within 60 days of the first.
Exclusions: cancelled orders, fully refunded orders, test and staff accounts.
Variants: separate subscription renewals from voluntary repeat purchases.
Reporting: cohort chart; latest complete cohort is 60 days old.
Risks: mix shift between channels; subscriptions inflating the rate.
questions.reference:
First, the question: do new customers come back and buy again? That suggests a cohort metric. For customers whose first completed order fell in a given week, the repeat purchase rate is the share who placed a second completed order — not cancelled, not fully refunded — within 60 days of their first. Staff and test accounts are excluded, and duplicate accounts merged where we can detect them.

The 60-day window means a cohort is only complete 60 days later, so the weekly dashboard shows a cohort chart: each week’s cohort at 30 and 60 days, with the most recent incomplete cohorts marked as such.

Subscriptions need care: an automatic renewal is not a decision to come back. I would report subscription renewals separately from voluntary repeat orders, otherwise a subscription launch inflates the rate without any change in loyalty. I would also watch channel mix: a promotion that brings in deal-seekers lowers the rate without anything being wrong with the product.
pitfalls: Mixing incomplete cohorts into a trend.

questions.title: Revenue that doubled overnight
questions.prompt: A colleague's query joins orders to order items and to promotions, then sums order totals by month. Revenue for last month came out almost twice the finance number. Explain the likely bug, how you would find it, and how to write the query correctly. (Describe the logic; executable SQL practice is in the Question Bank.)
hints: What is the grain of each table?
What happens to an order's total when it has three items?
How would you prove the fix is right?
followups: Some orders have two promotions. How does that affect your fix?
Finance counts revenue on shipment date, not order date. Does that explain the rest of the gap?
How would you prevent this class of bug?
criteria: Identifies fan-out: order-level totals repeated per item and per promotion.
Checks grain and row counts after each join.
Aggregates at the right grain before joining, or sums item-level amounts.
Validates against a trusted number and reconciles remaining differences (definitions, dates, refunds).
Suggests prevention (tests on grain, shared models).
outline: Grain: orders one row per order; items one per item; promotions possibly several per order.
Bug: summing order total after joining to items multiplies it by item count (and promotion count).
Find: count rows per order after joins; compare SUM(order_total) with SUM over distinct orders.
Fix: aggregate items and promotions to order level first, or sum item amounts; then join.
Validate: reconcile with finance; explain remaining differences (shipment date, refunds, tax).
Prevent: uniqueness tests on model grain; shared revenue model.
questions.reference:
The classic cause is fan-out. Orders have one row per order; order items have one row per item; promotions may have several rows per order. Joining orders to items repeats each order’s total once per item, and joining promotions multiplies it again. Summing the order total then counts each order several times.

To find it, I would check row counts after each join and count rows per order id; any order appearing more than once in a sum of order-level totals is the bug. A quick comparison of the sum over distinct orders against the joined sum shows the size of the error.

The fix is to aggregate at the right grain before joining: compute item-level and promotion-level figures per order in separate subqueries, then join one row per order — or sum item-level amounts instead of order totals. Then validate against finance. If a gap remains, it is usually a definition difference — finance may recognise revenue at shipment, exclude tax or net out refunds — which should be documented, not hidden. To prevent repeats, add uniqueness tests on each model’s grain and use one shared revenue model.
pitfalls: Using DISTINCT on the sum to hide the problem.

questions.title: Reading a messy test
questions.prompt: An experiment on a new search ranking shows: control 50,000 users, treatment 47,000 (it was meant to be 50/50). Treatment has +1.8% purchases per user with a confidence interval of −0.2% to +3.8%. A PM found that treatment won +6% among Android users. What do you conclude?
hints: What does the unequal split tell you?
What does an interval that crosses zero mean?
How many segments did the PM look at?
followups: Engineers find a bug: treatment users on old iOS versions crashed before logging. What now?
The PM still wants to ship to Android only. Respond.
What would you change for the rerun?
criteria: Flags the sample ratio mismatch first and investigates it before reading results.
Interprets the interval correctly (not significant at the stated level).
Treats the Android result as a possible multiple-comparisons artefact unless pre-registered.
Recommends fixing and rerunning, with a pre-registered plan.
Communicates clearly to the PM.
outline: Sample ratio mismatch: 47k vs 50k is very unlikely by chance → assignment or logging problem; results unreliable until explained.
Primary result: interval includes zero → no clear effect.
Segment: post-hoc segment wins are expected by chance when many are checked.
Action: find the SRM cause, fix, rerun with pre-registered metrics and segments.
If Android is a real hypothesis, test it directly.
questions.reference:
The first thing I see is the split: 47,000 versus 50,000 when it should be equal. A difference that large is very unlikely by chance, so something is wrong with assignment or logging — for example, treatment users crashing before they are counted. Until we know why, none of the results can be trusted, because the users missing from treatment are probably not random.

Even ignoring that, the main result is not conclusive: the interval runs from slightly negative to positive, so we cannot rule out no effect. The Android +6% is a classic trap: if you look at enough segments, some will look strong by chance. Unless Android was a pre-registered hypothesis, it is a lead, not a finding.

My recommendation: find and fix the cause of the mismatch, then rerun with the primary metric, guardrails and any segments written down in advance. If there is a genuine reason to expect Android to benefit, test that directly. I would tell the PM that this is not a ‘no’; it is ‘we do not know yet’.
pitfalls: Reading results before checking the split.

questions.title: Average order value fell
questions.prompt: Average order value on a food-delivery app fell 9% week over week. Nothing obvious shipped. Find out why.
hints: Is it a change in prices and basket size, or a change in who is ordering?
Check whether the drop is real first.
Which events could change mix: weather, promotions, holidays, a new city?
followups: Every city's average is flat, but the overall average fell. How?
Marketing launched a 'free delivery on small orders' promotion. Connect it.
Is a lower average order value bad?
criteria: Validates the data first.
Decomposes into rate vs mix (Simpson's paradox).
Segments systematically (city, channel, new vs returning, restaurant type, time of day).
Matches timing to events including marketing and external factors.
Concludes whether it is a problem, with evidence.
outline: Validate: pipeline, currency, refunds, definition.
Shape: sudden or gradual; which days.
Decompose: average = Σ segment share × segment average; did shares or averages change?
Segment: city, new vs returning, channel, cuisine, daypart, order type.
Events: promotions, weather, holidays, new market launches.
Conclude and assess impact on margin and orders.
questions.reference:
First I would rule out data problems: a currency conversion change, refunds counted differently, a pipeline delay.

Then decompose. An overall average can fall because averages fell within segments, or because the mix shifted toward segments with smaller orders, even if every segment is unchanged. If every city’s average is flat but the overall average fell, it is mix: for example, a new city with smaller orders, more lunch orders or more new customers.

I would segment by city, new versus returning customers, acquisition channel, time of day and order type, and line up the timing with events: weather, holidays, a new market, and promotions. A ‘free delivery on small orders’ promotion would explain it neatly — more small orders, lower average, possibly more total orders.

Whether it is bad depends on totals and margin: if order volume and total contribution rose, a lower average is the expected effect of a successful promotion. I would report the cause, the evidence and that judgement.
pitfalls: Calling a lower average bad without looking at totals.

questions.title: Five minutes with the VP
questions.prompt: Your analysis shows that customers who use the mobile app's new 'reorder' button spend 30% more — but most of that is because heavy customers adopted it first. The VP of Product wants to announce that the feature drives a 30% lift. You have five minutes with them. What do you say?
hints: Lead with what you are confident about.
How do you explain selection bias without jargon?
What can you offer instead of the 30% claim?
followups: The VP says 'close enough, the direction is right'. Respond.
What analysis would give a defensible number?
How do you keep the relationship good?
criteria: Leads with the conclusion and the risk of the claim.
Explains selection bias simply.
Offers a defensible estimate or a fast way to get one.
Respects the VP's goal (a positive story).
Documents caveats.
outline: Headline: the feature is popular with our best customers; the 30% is mostly who uses it, not what it does.
Plain explanation: heavy customers already spent more before using the button.
Better estimate: before/after for adopters vs similar non-adopters; or a holdout.
Offer: a defensible number in two weeks; meanwhile, announce adoption.
Write it down.
questions.reference:
I would lead with the answer: “The reorder button is a success with our best customers — but the 30% is mostly about who uses it, not what it does. If we announce 30%, someone will challenge it.”

Then explain simply: customers who adopted the button early were already our heaviest buyers; they spent more before they ever used it. Comparing them with everyone else measures that difference, not the button.

Then offer something useful. Comparing adopters’ spending before and after adoption, against similar customers who did not adopt, gives a more honest estimate — I can have it in about two weeks; a holdout test would be better still. Meanwhile, the VP can announce what is clearly true: strong adoption among top customers and how often they use it.

If they say the direction is right, I would agree the direction may be right but the size is not supported, and that a defensible number makes their story stronger. I would follow up in writing.
pitfalls: Only saying no without an alternative.

questions.title: An analysis that changed a decision
questions.prompt: Tell me about an analysis you did that changed what a team decided to do.
hints: What was the decision before your analysis?
What did you find, and how confident were you?
How did you get people to act?
criteria: Clear decision at stake.
Sound method with stated limitations.
Persuasive communication.
Measurable outcome.
Reflection.
outline: Decision and context.
Question and method.
Finding.
How you communicated.
Outcome.
Reflection.
questions.reference: A strong answer (a model of structure, not a script): “The team planned to build a loyalty programme because churn was high. I looked at cancellation reasons and order data, and found most churn followed late deliveries in two regions. I showed the team one chart: churn by number of late deliveries. They put the loyalty project on hold and worked with operations on delivery reliability in those regions. Churn there fell over the next quarter. In hindsight I would have shared the early finding sooner instead of waiting for a polished deck.”
